## Why

The coordinator's instructions and tool descriptions grew one issue at a time. Read together, in the coordinator's view file (`src/agent/coordinator.view.md`), they have gaps that make the agent's job harder than it needs to be, whatever model runs it. This issue collects those gaps, from Joe's review of the view file and an independent review of it, so they're fixed in one PR.

The bar for an item: a fix that's clearly good practice goes in here, with no evaluation needed first. That covers things a person using the same tools would need too, such as knowing what the app's terms mean. An item whose benefit is in doubt, such as one that adds tokens to every turn for a gain no one is sure of, isn't fixed here. It becomes a candidate for an agent evaluation instead.

## Design

- [Functional spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/functional-spec.md), section 4: the app's terms.
- [Technical spec](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/technical-spec.md), section 5.2: what the coordinator's instructions cover.
- [Tool design](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/blob/main/design/tools.md): the tool descriptions.

## Items

1. **The app's terms aren't defined for the coordinator.** The instructions define anchors and stretches (technical spec 4.1), but not the terms from functional spec 4 that the tools are built on: stay, night, day, last day, leg, stop, and candidate. The model pieces them together from tool descriptions. Example: `add_stay` says "Adds a stay, with one day for each of its nights", and a rule says "Only a day that starts and ends at the same stay can be a rest day". The riskiest gap is how nights and days add up. A 3-night stay covers three days, and the last day has no night, so a 7-day trip has 6 nights of stays. Nothing tells the model this. It could add 7 nights for a 7-day trip and get 8 days. The trip length check would catch it, but the model would be fixing a mistake it didn't need to make.

   The lines an itinerary read returns aren't explained either. Tool design section 4 says what an item means goes in the agent's instructions, and a read's lines are explained by the instructions. The trip brief follows this: the instructions explain each item, so `read_trip_brief` stays short. Nothing does the same for the itinerary. In a read of a day, nothing explains "in set 1", "Along the leg" or "Near the Springdale stay", "detour 38 m when offered", "with the drive buffer", "free time", or "Set time: 6:30 p.m." The `read_itinerary` description itself is fine. It says what each scope returns, which is specific to that tool.

   A few more terms need a line. "Set" as a noun ("2 in set 1") is one batch of candidates, and the option card shows only the newest set (functional spec 7.5). Without that, the coordinator may recommend a set 1 candidate the user can't see on the card. "Search area" is where a stop's places are looked for. "Last day" means the trip's final day in the check results rule, but the rule on removing a night says "Removing a night always removes the stay's last day," meaning the last of that stay's days. Say that one another way. Drive time is named three ways: "drive time" in the planning rounds, "road time" in `set_waypoints` and the reads, and "driving with the drive buffer" in the reads. Say what each is, so the model compares the right one with comfortableDrivingInHours.

   One repeat goes the other way. The bullets under "Reading the trip brief, the itinerary, and memory" say a whole read leaves out the rationale and the weather text, which the `read_itinerary` description already says. Tool design section 4 says the system prompt never repeats a tool's description.

   Fix: add a section on the itinerary to the instructions, like the one on the trip brief. It defines the terms, drawn from functional spec 4, and says what each line of a read means. Drop the repeat from the reading bullets, and keep the rules there on when to read a stop or stay. Add the section to the list in technical spec 5.2.

   Then review every tool description against the new section, so each term is defined in one place and used the same way everywhere. `compute_route` needs it most. Its description says "A stop is where the party stops, such as a town that might become a stay," and its points take a kind of "stop" or "passThrough". In the itinerary, a stop is a meal or attraction on a day, not a town. It also says "pass-through point" where `set_waypoints` says "waypoint" for the same idea.

2. **The rule for places the user names says to always call `find_in_trip` first, with no reason given.** `find_in_trip` exists because a whole read names only the selected places. It only counts the other candidates, so the coordinator doesn't know their names. The rule leaves that out, and it's broader than technical spec 7.1, which says to look up only "a name it can't find in context." As written, it sends the coordinator to `find_in_trip` for a place it already has an ID for, such as a selected restaurant from the whole read, and for a place that's clearly new to the trip. It also says to ask the user when no match is clearly the place, which fits a typo such as "Desert Rose", but not a place that isn't in the trip. `find_in_trip` always returns the 5 closest places, so when the user says "let's add Arches" on a trip with no Arches, none is close, and the rule has the coordinator ask "Did you mean Desert View Watchtower?" Fix: give the reason, and split the rule into three cases. For a place the coordinator already has an ID for, use it. For a place it doesn't have, that may be one the trip offered, use `find_in_trip`. Ask the user when a match is close but may not be the place. When none is close, the place isn't in the trip, so use `find_place`. For a place that's new to the trip, use `find_place`. Skipping `find_in_trip` for a new place is safe, since `select_user_place` refuses a place that's already a candidate on that stop, and its reply names any other stop or stay where the place is a candidate. Proposed wording, to replace the first bullet under "Places the user names" and change the second:

   > A whole read names only the selected places. It only counts the other candidates, so you won't know their names unless a scoped read or a worker's reply showed them.
   > - When the user names a place you already have an ID for, use it.
   > - When they name one you don't have, and it may be a place the trip offered, look for it with find_in_trip. When a match is close but you aren't sure it's the place, ask the user, such as "Did you mean the Desert Pearl Inn, the hotel in Springdale?" for "Desert Rose". A shorter form of a name, such as "the Desert Pearl" for the Desert Pearl Inn, is clear, so don't ask. When none is close, the place isn't in the trip, so look it up with find_place.
   > - For a place that's new to the trip, such as one a friend recommended, use find_place.

   Change technical spec 5.2 ("When the user names a place") and tool design 2.1 ("`find_in_trip` finds a place the user names") to match.

3. **The rule on when to raise warnings is unclear.** It says "Raise warnings at the end of the turn, for those still open, once no change is still being discussed with the user." "At the end of the turn" sounds like every turn, and "a change" is vague. It could be read as holding warnings until the whole trip is planned. It means holding them until the change the coordinator and the user are working on is settled, which can take several turns. The weather worker rule in technical spec 5.2 uses the same phrase and has an example. The coordinator's line has none. Fix: replace the line with this wording, and change technical spec 5.2 ("How to handle broken feasibility rules") to match:

   > Raise warnings once a change is settled, not while you and the user are still working it out. A change can take several turns, such as adding a night and then going through the stops it moved. Raise them at the end of the turn where the user confirms the change or backs out of it, and only those still open. Example: adding a Big Sur night makes a 3-day trip 4 days. Don't raise the trip length while you're still going through the stops the night moved. If the user then removes the night, the warning is gone, and there's nothing to raise.

4. **`add_stay`'s description says where the stay goes in a way that only makes sense next to the input schema.** It says "Adds a stay, with one day for each of its nights, after the stay given or first." "The stay given" and "first" point to the `after` input without naming it, and "first" isn't quoted, though the input's description quotes it. The next sentence uses "first" again, with another meaning: "Needs the itinerary's start place, end place, and start date first." Fix: name the input, and say what "first" does. A starting point:

   > Adds a stay, with one day for each of its nights. Give after the ID of the stay it follows, or "first" to put it before every other stay. The place is usually a town. The itinerary's start place, end place, and start date must be set before a stay can be added.

   Check `update_stay`'s "where it goes" the same way. `add_stops` and `move_stop` aren't built yet, but take an `after` input too (tool design 2.1, "Where an item goes"). Add a line to tool design 2.1 that a description names the `after` input and says what "first" does, so they follow the same pattern.

5. **`update_day`'s start time takes "none" to mean the trip brief's usual start time.** "None" reads as "no start time," which isn't what it does. The day still starts at the usual start time. Fix: take "default" instead, for a day's start time only. A stop's set time keeps "none" (tool design 2.1, "Times are clock times"), since a stop with no set time really has none. Today only the start time uses `NO_TIME` in `src/tools/skeleton-input.schema.ts`, since the stop tools aren't built yet. Rename it for "default", and change tool design 2.1 to match.

6. **`find_place`'s description says "When you aren't sure where the place is, give its state."** The sentence is about the `where` input, but doesn't name it. It means: when you don't know the town, give the state rather than guess a town. It reads as if the state were optional. And `where` takes "a town, region, or state," so a region with no state, such as "Big Sur", is allowed, though it's the case where the state helps most. The app plans only US trips, so every place has a state. Fix: drop the sentence from the description, and say it in `where`'s input description instead. A starting point:

   > A town or region with its state, or only the state when you aren't sure where the place is, such as "Moab, UT", "Big Sur, CA", or "Utah".

   Change the `find_place` row in tool design 2.3 to match.

7. **The instructions describe a write's check results differently from what the tools return.** "Tools that change the trip" says each write "replies with the feasibility check results the change made new, changed, or gone, anywhere in the trip." The reply (`src/tools/check-results-reply.ts`) also lists the already-known results for what the write touched, and marks a warning the user approved as "approved", such as "New warning, approved: …". The instructions never say what "approved" means, what "open" means in "warnings that are still open", or that a warning must be raised while a note is the coordinator's call (technical spec 8). Example: after a write, the coordinator sees "New warning, approved: Day 4 drives 7 h", and raises a warning the user already accepted. Fix: say what the reply lists, as technical spec 8 does ("What comes back"). Say each result is a warning or a note: a warning must be raised, and whether to mention a note is up to the coordinator. Say a warning marked approved is one the user accepted, so it isn't open, and isn't raised again.

8. **The memory section contradicts itself.** It says user memory holds standing preferences "such as their usual driving hours, route preference, budget, meal habits". Then "Writing memory" says "Don't save what the trip brief or the itinerary holds", and the trip brief holds those items for this trip. Example: the user says "we never drive more than 5 hours, on any trip." The coordinator sets comfortableDrivingInHours and skips user memory, so the next trip doesn't know. The rule is meant for trip memory. Fix: make it "Don't save to trip memory what the trip brief or the itinerary holds". The rule is only in `src/agent/coordinator-prompt.ts`, so add it to the "Writing memory" bullets in technical spec 5.2 too.

9. **Nothing tells the coordinator to keep IDs out of chat.** Technical spec 7.1 says "Users never see IDs." Every read and write reply is full of them, such as `stop_k7m2x9qa`, and the only rule about IDs in the instructions is for memory items. Example: "I moved breakfast (stop_k7m2x9qa) to Day 3." Fix: add to Conduct, such as "Never show IDs to the user. Name places, days, and stops in words." Add it to the conduct bullet in technical spec 5.2.

10. **"Where the road is still open" reads as a road closure.** The skeleton bullet says "set waypoints on scenic legs where the road is still open". It means the part of a leg that no stop the user chose already decides (technical spec 4.2: "The route preference is for the stretches nobody has decided"). "Open" also means an unsettled warning elsewhere in the instructions. Example: the coordinator checks for seasonal closures, and sets scenic waypoints on a leg whose road the user's own stops already chose. Fix: say "where no stop the user chose already decides the road", and change technical spec 4.2 to match.

11. **`find_place` says "Every match is saved to the trip."** Item 2 uses "in the trip" to mean in the itinerary, and `find_in_trip` searches only the itinerary. A place `find_place` saved isn't in it. Example: after a `find_place` lookup, the coordinator expects `find_in_trip` to find the place later, and it doesn't. Fix: "Every match is stored, so its place ID works in the other tools. That doesn't add it to the itinerary."

12. **`remove_stay` says it's "Refused while any stop is on its days, or any stop anywhere is near it."** "Near it" sounds like distance on a map. It means a stop on another day whose search area is this stay. Fix: say that.

13. **Some text is repeated between the instructions and the tool descriptions,** which tool design section 4 says never to do, since the copies can drift apart:
    - "Stays can't be added until all three are set" in the discovery round, and `add_stay`'s "Needs the itinerary's start place, end place, and start date first."
    - "Only a day that starts and ends at the same stay can be a rest day" in "Days and approvals", and the same in `update_day`.
    - "Removing a night always removes the stay's last day" in "Changes to stays", and `update_stay`'s "Changing the nights adds or removes days at the end of the stay's days."
    - The `tierRule` input's "The rule that produced the tier", which says what the item means. By tool design section 4 that belongs only in the instructions, which already say it in the skeleton bullet on tiers. The input gives only the format.

    Fix: keep each fact in one place. Where a rule in the instructions depends on one, such as the advice on losing a different day when a night is removed, it can rely on the description instead of repeating it.

14. **The rule for a refused trip brief update conflicts with the limit rules.** It says "If the error gives a limit, such as the maximum daily driving, send the whole update again with that item at the limit, and tell the user it's set to the maximum." The rules on trip length and comfortable driving hours say to push back instead: propose a trip that fits, or recommend fewer hours and ask what's comfortable. The refusal only happens once the coordinator has already ignored the limit in its instructions and in the input's description, and the error gives the limit too. So a fourth place that says what to do adds nothing, and the coordinator can judge what to do next. Fix: drop that sentence. Keep "nothing in it was saved", which tells the coordinator to send the other items again. That's specific to this tool, so move it into `update_trip_brief`'s description, and drop the bullet from the instructions. Change technical spec 5.2 and the `setComfortableDriving()` refusal in domain model 4.2, which says "so the coordinator can send it again at the limit", to match.

15. **The coordinator can't see whether "the route already goes through" an area.** The skeleton bullet on must-see areas says to add a waypoint "unless the route already goes through." No tool returns a route's path, only times and distances. Fix: say it's a judgment from the coordinator's own knowledge of the roads, such as UT-24 running through Capitol Reef, and to add the waypoint when it isn't sure.

16. **Nothing says what to do when the user asks to forget a trip brief item.** The instructions say "Trip brief items can be changed, but not forgotten," and that when the user asks to forget an item, forget it, which is about memory. Fix, as a starting point:

    > When the user asks to forget a trip brief item, explain that it can be changed but not forgotten. For restDaysText or budgetRulesText, change its text to say there's none, such as "no budget rules."

    Only these two optional text items can say there's none. A required item can't, as item 17 says.

17. **Nothing says what "required" means for a trip brief item.** The instructions say each item is required except three, and to establish each one. They don't say what to do when the user says "we don't really have any interests" or "no must-sees". A model could save "none" and move on. The app plans trips to see and do things, not only routes between hotels, so "none" isn't an answer for a required item. Fix, as a starting point:

    > Required means a real answer. When the user has none, help them find one, such as by suggesting what the focus is known for. Don't save "none".

18. **"Confirm it and push back" can read as accept it.** The rule on comfortable driving hours says "When the user gives more than 6, confirm it and push back." "Confirm" can mean accept and save it. It means check that they mean it. Fix: "check that they mean it, and push back". Change functional spec 5.2 and technical spec 5.2, which say "confirms it and pushes back", to match.

More items are added here as the review goes on.

## Open questions

- None. The implementer writes a first draft of all new wording, and Joe gives feedback on it in the PR.

## Do

- Write a first draft of the new wording for each item, including item 1's itinerary section. Wording given in any item is a starting point, not settled text.
- Make each item's fix in the coordinator's instructions (`src/agent/coordinator-prompt.ts`), the tool descriptions, and the design doc each one belongs in.
- Run `npm run agent-views`, and commit the coordinator's view file with the change.

## Done when

- The coordinator's view file shows each item's fix.
- The design docs match the instructions and tool descriptions.
- `npm run check` passes.

## Ends in

A PR.

**Settled in:** the PR.

Example: `add_stay` says "Adds a stay, with one day for each of its nights", and a rule says "Only a day that starts and ends at the same stay can be a rest day". The riskiest gap is how nights and days add up. A 3-night stay covers three days, and the last day has no night, so a 7-day trip has 6 nights of stays. Nothing tells the model this. It could add 7 nights for a 7-day trip and get 8 days. The trip length check would catch it, but the model would be fixing a mistake it didn't need to make. Fix: add a short terms section near the start of the instructions, drawn from functional spec 4, and add it to the list in technical spec 5.2.
